name: capabilities
description: Access capabilities: what you may do, why something was denied, and how to grant bounded authority via UCAN. Load on 'no access capability' or a denial.

content.inline:
## Access capabilities & granting
An **access capability** is what lets you read or do one thing. Lacking one is what `no access capability` and `Capability denied` both mean — the resource may well exist; you simply hold no grant covering it. Neither is fixed by retrying: check what you hold, use a resource you do have access to, or ask whoever owns it for a grant.

A capability is a `{with, can}` pair: `with` names a resource (a path prefix such as `w/reports/`, a DID URL, or a scheme resource), `can` names an ability (`crud/read`, `crud/write`, `asset/read`, `asset/store`, `invoke`, plus adapter-specific ones). `crud/write` changes what is at its path; creating a new key, file or drive also needs it on the map or directory that holds it. Every operation checks its own at the point of action; a denial reads `Capability denied` and names the resource that failed, which is what tells you what to ask for.

Delegation is a UCAN token:
- Issue `{aud, att, exp}` — the audience DID receives the attenuated capabilities `att` until `exp`. Grant the MINIMUM: the narrowest resource prefix and the shortest expiry that does the job. A token you cannot justify is one you should not issue.
- Verify `{token, with?, can?, aud?}` checks a presented token before you rely on it.
- Present tokens in the request envelope (`ucans`); body-less reads carry them on the `X-Covia-Ucans` header instead.

Attenuation only ever narrows within a delegation chain. A chain can drop rights at each hop and never add them, so nothing you pass on can exceed what that chain grants. Separate grant sources combine additively, within any access-token and callable caps. A gated grant is not a global deny rule: an unconditional covering grant can authorise. Issuing is itself a right: granting surfaces require `grant/<ability>`, so being able to USE an ability does not imply being able to GIVE it.

What this means in practice:
- An agent's tool actions use its controller's authority narrowed by current config.caps; presented UCANs add rights within any token/callable narrowing. Configured model calls are harness work under the controller's authority, not the agent's tool caps.
- Loading a skill grants no resource authority. Admitting skills or tools outside the advertised surface needs explicit skill/load or tool/load on the reference, even when otherwise unrestricted. Bound tools enforce their resource abilities; generic lookup additionally requires invoke. A family grant is crud or agent, not crud/* or agent/*. Only nb.gate and nb.url are implemented caveats; unknown caveats fail closed.
- Anonymous access follows the venue's public policy; its default is read-only on the public principal's own namespace plus asset/read, but the operator can change it or disable access.
- If no inherent or presented grant gives you a right, ask the human who owns the resource rather than working around it — an approved request can mint exactly the grant needed.

Job permissions are independent: job/read observes the Job record and result, job/manage controls its lifecycle, and job/message delivers input. Grants name the owner DID and j/<Job ID>; job is the umbrella ability. Creating a Job or loading tools grants no continuing Job authority. Raw CRUD rights do not authorize Job operations. Controls return an acknowledgement, not the result. Supply owner for another user's retained Job. Grant only the needed abilities and resource; use a host URL constraint for access limited to one venue.
